newsitem.title: TAIWAN: FOCUS-Taiwan hikes key rates, stocks seen tumbling.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Taiwan hikes key rates, stocks seen tumbling.

text.p: Taiwan's central bank announced on Thursday a modest tightening of monetary policy by raising two key rates, and analysts said the surprise move could chill the stock exchange -- at least for the time being.

While carefully avoiding saying so, central bank governor Sheu Yuan-dong left little doubt in comments after a board meeting that the central bank was worried the stock market's punch past 10,000 on Thursday was too much too soon.

"Whether the stock market is too high should be determined by investors and the market. But as to whether the market is overheated..., the stock turnover rate is too high, but whether 10,000 points is reasonable or not, I've no opinion," he said.
Analysts said they expected a sharp stock market reaction.

"The stock market will definitely fall tomorrow," said HSBC James Capel analyst Alex Chen. "It's obvious the central bank wants to clamp down speculation -- not only in the forex market but in the stock market."

National Securities international sales chief Oliver Fang said: "The unexpected rate hikes caught everyone by surprise. The market always reacts drastically to the unexpected. The index will fall at least 200 points at the open tomorrow."

A Reuters Financial Television straw poll taken after the stock market closed -- but before the central bank meeting -- forecast the index eclipsing its historic high of 12,495 in the third quarter and ending 1997 at around 10,792.
Sheu said the bank decided to raise the rediscount rate to 5.25 percent from 5.00 and accommodations against secured loans to 5.625 percent from 5.375, effective from Friday.
Sheu described the central bank's adjusted monetary policy as "not loose, not tight", a slight tightening from his own longtime refrain of "stable to loose, but not too loose".
"All the board members agreed that we should make a small adjustment," Sheu said. "This is a bit different from our previous monetary policy. You could call it fine-tuning."
At least one analyst was amused by Sheu's attempt to have monetary policy tight and loose at the same time.

"The new monetary policy is a joke," said Nomura Securities analyst Amy Huang. "No other country in the world has this kind of monetary policy. You either have a tight or loose monetary policy. It can't be something in between."

Sheu pledged to respect market forces in the stock market as well as the foreign exchange market, where the Taiwan dollar has plunged four percent this week. The currency ended at T$28.7 to the U.S. dollar, its lowest level since 1988.

Sheu insisted that the bank would rely only on macroeconomic money-supply levers to regulate the availability of liquidity in the economy and would leave the Taiwan dollar exchange rate and stock market at the mercy of market forces -- with one caveat.

"The bank will...let market supply and demand determine the Taiwan dollar exchange rates. But if there are abnormal factors intervening in the market it will adopt appropriate measures to maintain the foreign exchange market's stability," he said.
Sheu did not define "appropriate measures".
Sheu said the Taiwan dollar's dramatic depreciation did not appear to have resulted from speculative attacks like those that have bedevilled Southeast Asia's currencies in July.

Sheu said the central bank's repeated recent issuance of billions of Taiwan dollars worth of negotiable certificates of deposit was not intended to cool the stock exchange -- something that many brokers and money dealers have asserted.
The stock market has been on an almost unbroken streak since mid-1996, with the index more than doubling in value in that period with the island's electronics sector leading the way.
After a failed bid on Tuesday, the index on Thursday surged comfortably through psychological resistance at 10,000 points to close at 10,066.35, its highest close since early 1990.
